etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English roren, raren, from Old English rārian (“to roar; wail; lament”), from Proto-West Germanic *rairōn, from Proto-Germanic *rairōną (“to bellow; roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *rey- (“to shout; bellow; yell; bark”), perhaps of imitative origin.

Cognate with Saterland Frisian roorje (“to roar”), German röhren (“to roar”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make a loud, deep cry, especially from pain, anger, or other strong emotion.

quote.citation: a. 1701 (date written), John Dryden, “The First Book of Homer’s Ilias”, in The Miscellaneous Works of John Dryden, […], volume IV, London:  […]  J[acob] and R[ichard] Tonson, […], published 1760, →OCLC, page 434:
quote.text: Sole on the barren ſands the ſuff'ring chief / Roar'd out for anguiſh, and indulg'd his grief.

definitions.definition: To laugh in a particularly loud manner.
Of animals (especially a lion), to make a loud deep noise.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto VI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, , stanzas 6-7, page 14:
quote.text: Roaring bulls he would him make to tame.

definitions.definition: Generally, of inanimate objects etc., to make a loud resounding noise.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book X”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: The brazen throat of war had ceased to roar.

quote.citation: [1716], [John] Gay, “(please specify the page number(s))”, in Trivia: Or, The Art of Walking the Streets of London, London:  […]  Bernard Lintott, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: How oft I crossed where carts and coaches roar.

quote.citation: 2011 January 25, Phil McNulty, “Blackpool 2-3 Man Utd”, in BBC:
quote.text: United's attempt to extend their unbeaten league sequence to 23 games this season looked to be in shreds as the Seasiders - managed by Ian Holloway - roared into a fully deserved two-goal lead at the interval.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cry aloud; to proclaim loudly.

quote.text: This last action will roar thy infamy.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I made a speaking trumpet of my hands and commenced to whoop “Ahoy!” and “Hello!” at the top of my lungs.  […]  The Colonel woke up, and, after asking what in brimstone was the matter, opened his mouth and roared “Hi!” and “Hello!” like the bull of Bashan.

definitions.definition: To be boisterous; to be disorderly.

quote.citation: 1724, Gilbert Burnet, History of My Own Time:
quote.text: It was a mad, roaring time, full of extravagance.

definitions.definition: To make a loud noise in breathing, as horses do when they have a certain disease.
(British Yorkshire, North Midlands, informal) To cry.

quote.citation: 1886, James Orchard Halliwell, “Third Class: Tales: LX”, in The Nursery Rhymes of England:
quote.text: Tom, Tom, the piper's son,Stole a pig, and away he run!The pig was eat, and Tom was beat,And Tom went roaring down the street.

definitions.definition: A long, loud, deep shout, as of rage or laughter, made with the mouth wide open.

quote.citation: 1900 May 17, L[yman] Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chicago, Ill.; New York, N.Y.: Geo[rge] M[elvin] Hill Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: The Winkies were not a brave people, but they had to do as they were told. So they marched away until they came near to Dorothy. Then the Lion gave a great roar and sprang towards them, and the poor Winkies were so frightened that they ran back as fast as they could.

definitions.definition: The deep cry of the bull.

quote.citation: 1944, Ernie Pyle, Brave Men, University of Nebraska Press (2001), page 107:
quote.text: "Those lovely valleys and mountains were filled throughout the day and night with the roar of heavy shooting."

definitions.definition: A show of strength or character.
